newsitem.title: UK: Doctors finally figure out why carrots are good.
newsitem.headline: Doctors finally figure out why carrots are good.

text.p: British doctors said on Tuesday they had finally figured out what it is about carrots that helps fight off cancer.
They said beta-carotene, which gives vegetables like carrots and broccoli their deep colour, helped stimulate a molecule that helps the immune system target and destroy cancer cells.

Volunteers who took beta-carotene supplements equivalent to three or four carrots a day for a month showed a "significant" increase in the number of the molecules, the researchers told Biochemical Society and British Society for Immunology in Harrogate, northern England.

David Hughes and colleagues at the Institute of Food Research in Norwich said the beta-carotene increased the number of receptors on white blood cells for a molecule known as major histocompatibility complex II (MHC II).

Cancerous cells have different proteins on their surfaces from normal cells. Immune system cells known as killer T-cells or CD8 cells use such surface proteins to identify foreign invaders or cancer cells.
Other immune system cells known as monocytes help direct the CD8 cells and they use MHC II to do this.
While scientists agree that eating vegetables helps fight cancer, debate has continued over whether beta-carotene supplements do the same.

Research has shown that antioxidant vitamins such as vitamin A reduce cancer risks. But some studies of people given supplements of beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A, showed no beneficial effect and some showed possible harm.
Two studies over the past year, one Finnish and one in the United States, showed that beta-carotene supplements slightly increased the risk of lung cancer in long-term smokers.
But a third U.S. study found beta-carotene supplements helped reverse incidences of oral leukoplakia, which can progress to oral cancer.

Hughes's group was small -- only 24 volunteers -- and the study would have to be duplicated in a larger group. But he said his findings could mean beta-carotene could help the body fight off infections as well as cancer.
